items.a: Traditional architectural documentation — historical plans and sections — with terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) surveys of five Gothic cathedrals: Girona, Mallorca, Narbonne, Laon and Chartres.

items.q: Why do historical drawings differ from the built cathedrals?
items.a: Because they rely on idealised geometries: they tend to correct deviations, regularise axes and simplify irregularities produced by long construction processes, and they served representational and interpretative rather than strictly metric purposes.

items.q: What does terrestrial laser scanning add?
items.a: Highly accurate 3D point clouds that record deformations, asymmetries, construction tolerances and geometric variations that traditional surveying rarely captures.

items.q: How was the comparison carried out?
items.a: The historical documents were redrawn in CAD; plans, sections and orthoimages were extracted from the point clouds and vectorised; the two were then aligned and overlaid in a common reference system, using pier axes and the nave axis in plan, and floor lines, imposts, arch springing and keystones in section.

items.q: Which instruments and campaigns were used?
items.a: Leica RTC360 for Girona (2019), Mallorca (2021) and Narbonne (2023), and Leica BLK for Chartres and Laon (2026), with registration errors of a few millimetres and photogrammetry in some cases.

items.q: How closely do the drawings match the scans?
items.a: In plan there is a high degree of overall agreement: discrepancies are mostly slight deviations in pier alignment, small variations in bay spacing and minor differences in walls and side chapels, consistent with medieval construction tolerances.
In section, in the parameters hardest to measure by hand: nave heights, the exact positions of vault keystones and the actual curvature of some arches.
Narbonne, both in plan and in section, particularly in elements of the central nave and the east end.

items.q: Does the article set digital survey against historical drawing?
items.a: No. It treats them as complementary: traditional drawings explain the design logic of Gothic architecture, while TLS tests those geometries against the building as constructed.
